title: Hubble Sees a Cosmic Caterpillar
caption: Protostar IRAS 20324+4057, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Isaac Newton Telescope
celestial: IRAS 20324+4057 · constellation Cygnus · about 4,500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA), and IPHAS

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A knot of gas and dust a light-year long stretches across this view like a caterpillar heading for a meal. The object, IRAS 20324+4057, is a protostar, a star at a very early stage of growth, lying 4,500 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus.

Its shape is imposed from outside. Toward the right edge of the image, 15 light-years from the knot, are 65 O-type stars, among the hottest and brightest known. With 500 fainter but still highly luminous B-type stars they make up the Cygnus OB2 association, thought to hold more than 30,000 times the mass of our Sun. Their winds and ultraviolet radiation are sculpting the knot into its long shape and wearing it away.

That erosion matters for the star inside. Spectra show the central star still drawing heavily on its envelope of gas. Protostars here should grow to about one to ten times the Sun's mass, but if radiation destroys the envelope first, they may end up lighter.

understand.summary: A composite of Hubble Advanced Camera for Surveys data and ground-based hydrogen-alpha images from the Isaac Newton Telescope. H-alpha is shown in cyan, F606W in blue and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The F814W layer records infrared light that the eye cannot see, and the H-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen alone.

explore: The protostar is still collecting material from the gas envelope around it, and whether it ends up a heavyweight or a lightweight star is not yet settled. The picture blends Hubble data from 2006, taken in green and infrared light, with ground-based hydrogen observations from the Isaac Newton Telescope in 2003, gathered for the IPHAS survey.
